key: How know I that it is so with all the beauties of existing things? By this (nature of the Tao).
s: The chapter asks how it is known that it is so with all the beauties of existing things, and answers, by this; Wang Bi, on chapter 21, reads the question as how it is known that all things begin in non-being, and takes ‘this’ as the chapter’s preceding account of the nameless, through which all things come to be.
src: Wang Bi, Laozi zhu, chapter 21, zh.wikisource (the Huating Zhang edition), revision 2354026 (2024)

opened.edition: zh.wikisource 道德經 (王弼本), the 華亭張氏 edition, revision 2354026
opened.locator: chapter 21, comments on 自今及古，其名不去, 以閱眾甫 and 吾何以知眾甫之狀哉？以此

evidence.words: 至真之極，不可得名，無名則是其名也。自古及今，無不由此而成 … 眾甫，物之始也。以無名說萬物始也。 … 此上之所云也。言吾何以知萬物之始於無哉，以此知之也。
evidence.gloss: The utmost of the truly real cannot be named; being nameless is its name. From of old until now nothing has not come to completion through this … ‘The many fathers’ are the beginning of things: the text explains the beginning of all things by the nameless. … ‘This’ is what has been said above. It means: how do I know that all things begin in non-being? I know it by this.

reason: The critic is right that ‘what has been said above’ is a pointer without content. Wang Bi’s comment on the immediately preceding lines supplies it: the utmost real cannot be named, its name is the nameless, nothing from of old till now has come to completion except through it, and the text explains the beginning of all things by the nameless; his comment on 以此 then says ‘this’ is what was said above. The corrected sentence names that content (the chapter’s preceding account of the nameless, through which all things come to be) from those words only.
